procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant challenged the Assistant Registrar's order by filing a Writ Petition to the High Court of Patna, which was dismissed. Later, the High Court at Patna found the appellant guilty of contempt and sentenced him to simple imprisonment until the rising of the court and a fine of Rs. 200.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court after the Patna High Court upheld the contempt charge against him.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies was functioning as a court in deciding the dispute in question.

facts: The Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies decided a dispute under Section 48 of the Bihar and Orissa Co-operative Societies Act, 1935.
The Assistant Registrar was exercising the powers of the Registrar, which had been delegated to him by the State Government under Section 6(2) of the Act.
law: Under Rule 68(10) of the Bihar and Orissa Co-operative Societies Rules, 1959, the Registrar (and by delegation, the Assistant Registrar) has the same powers as a civil court under the Code of Civil Procedure when trying a suit, including the power to summon witnesses and compel the production of documents.
application: The Court distinguished this case from others where a Registrar acted merely as an arbitrator based on a private reference. Here, the Assistant Registrar was exercising statutory powers.
The Court rejected the argument that the Assistant Registrar was like an arbitrator, noting that the procedure for referring a dispute to an arbitrator was not followed in this case.

The Court found that the Assistant Registrar's adjudication was not a summary decision but was conducted with "all the paraphernalia of a court" and he was vested with the powers of an ordinary civil court.
The decision was explicitly limited to the specific context of the Bihar and Orissa Co-operative Societies Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that the Assistant Registrar was functioning as a court because his adjudication was not based on a private reference, and under the relevant Act and Rules, he was vested with and exercised the powers of an ordinary civil court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Assistant Registrar of Co-operative Societies was functioning as a court in deciding the dispute in question.
appellant_arguments: The Assistant Registrar was not a court, but was acting as an arbitrator, similar to the facts of previous cases in Bombay and Allahabad.
The Assistant Registrar was merely acting on a dispute transferred to him for disposal by the Registrar, implying a delegated, non-judicial function.
respondent_arguments: The Assistant Registrar was a court subordinate to the High Court for the purpose of the Contempt of Courts Act.
As a tribunal under the superintendence of the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution, there is no distinction between it and a civil court for the purposes of contempt.
The Assistant Registrar was not acting as an arbitrator but was discharging the statutory functions of the Registrar under delegated authority from the State Government.

The proceedings before the Assistant Registrar involved the essential attributes of a court, such as the presentation of cases by parties, the ascertainment of facts through evidence, and the submission of legal arguments.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For the purpose of Section 3 of the Contempt of Courts Act, subordination means judicial subordination. A court or tribunal is judicially subordinate to the High Court if it is subject to the High Court's power of superintendence under Article 227 of the Constitution, not merely if it is part of the hierarchy of courts under the Civil Procedure Code or the Criminal Procedure Code.
obiter: The power of revision conferred upon the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution is similar in nature to its appellate power, though circumscribed by limitations.

Article 228 of the Constitution, which allows a High Court to withdraw a case involving a substantial question of constitutional interpretation, is not the determinative test for whether a lower court is subordinate to the High Court.
There is no reason or principle to distinguish between a civil court subordinate to the High Court and a tribunal subordinate to the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.

To decide in a judicial manner involves that the parties are entitled to be heard and adduce evidence, and it imports an obligation on the authority to decide the matter on a consideration of the evidence and in accordance with law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: For the purposes of the Contempt of Courts Act, there is no reason or principle to distinguish between a civil court subordinate to the High Court and a tribunal, such as the Assistant Registrar, which is subordinate to the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution. If a body possesses the essential attributes of a court—where parties have a right to be heard and adduce evidence, and the authority has an obligation to decide based on that evidence and in accordance with law—it functions as a court and is protected by contempt laws.
legal_tests_applied: When a question therefore arises as to whetller an autllority created by an Act is a court as distinguished from a quasi-judicial tribunal, what has to be decided is whetller having regard to tlle provisions of the Act it possesses all the attributes of a court.

The attributes of a court include that parties are entitled as a matter of right to be heard in support of their claim and to adduce evidence in proof of it, and it also imports an obligation on the part of the authority to decide the matter on a consideration of the evidence adduced and in accordance with law.

In determining whether a tribunal is a judicial body, elements to be considered are (1) the requirement for a public hearing, subject to a power to exclude the public in a proper case, and (2) a provision that a member of the tribunal shall not take part in any decision in which he is personally interested, or unless he has been present throughout the proceedings.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the notion that a body is not subordinate to the High Court simply because a case cannot be withdrawn from it under Article 228 of the Constitution, stating that the article is not the sole indicator of subordination.

The court's finding that the Assistant Registrar possessed the essential attributes of a court and was a tribunal under the superintendence of the High Court under Article 227 directly negated the appellant's claim that the officer was merely an arbitrator or acting in a non-judicial capacity.
why_respondent_won: The court accepted that there was no reason or principle on which any distinction could be drawn between a civil court which was subordinate to the High Court and a tribunal which was subordinate to the High Court under Art. 227 of the Constitution for the purposes of contempt.

The court determined that the proceedings before the Assistant Registrar possessed the essential attributes of a court, as parties had the right to be heard and present evidence, and the authority was obligated to decide the matter based on that evidence and in accordance with the law.
policy_considerations: In order that courts should be able to dispense justice without fear or favour, affection or ill-will, it is essential that litigants who resort to courts should so conduct themselves as not to bring the authority and the administration of law into disrespect or disregard.

This principle applies equally to all Judges and all litigants irrespective of the status of the Judge, i.e., whether he occupies one of the highest judicial offices in the land or is the presiding officer of a court of very limited jurisdiction.

As the Contempt of Courts Act, 1952 does not define 'courts', in the interest of justice any conduct of contempt towards any person who can be called a 'court' should be amenable to the jurisdiction under the Act.
